rows: Cuticle: waxy protective layer on top of the epidermis, which reduces the loss of water and stops the leaf from drying out.
Upper epidermis: outer protective layer. Carries out gas exchange. Has a few stomata to help prevent water loss.
Palisade layer: contains cells with chloroplasts. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and are placed where they receive a lot of light for photosynthesis.
Vascular bundle (leaf vein): contains phloem and xylem cells. Xylem transports water and minerals to the leaf, and phloem takes sugar (glucose) away from the leaf to other parts of the plant.
Spongy mesophyll: this is where gas exchange takes place. Carbon dioxide enters and oxygen is released.
Guard cells: these regulate the balance between water loss and carbon dioxide uptake.
Stomata: tiny openings bordered by guard cells in the epidermis of leaves and stems. Gases pass through stomata.
Nitrogen: Older leaves on the plants start to turn yellow.
Phosphorus: Older leaves will turn yellow and start to fall off. There may be dead areas on the leaf.
Potassium: Leaf turns yellow with small brown spots developing. Young leaves have yellowing on their edges.
Healthy: Green leaves that have a shiny sheen to them.
Magnesium: Both old and new leaves will turn pale. However the veins will remain green.
Iron: Leaves are pale in colour. The leaf can become almost transparent.

rows: Mulberry tree bark: The primary material for tapa cloth comes from the inner bark of the mulberry tree. This bark is fibrous and needs to be harvested carefully to avoid damaging the tree.
Water: Water is essential for soaking the bark to soften it and make it easier to work with.
Natural dyes: Different plants and materials can be used to create natural dyes for colouring the tapa cloth. Common sources of dyes include plants, roots, barks, and even charcoal for black.
Beating board: The anvil or beating board provides a hard, flat surface for laying the bark during the beating process. It helps distribute the force of the mallet evenly.
Tapa beaters/Wooden mallets: These are used to beat and pound the mulberry tree bark. They help soften and stretch the fibres, making the material thinner and more flexible.
Tools: Various tools can be used to create patterns and designs on the tapa cloth.
Knife or scrapers: To remove the outer bark and separate the inner bark layers, a sharp knife or shell scraper is used.

rows: How this is demonstrated by the Montgomery Bus Boycott 1955–1956

This concept is demonstrated by Martin Luther King Jr. because he was able to motivate the African American community in Montgomery to boycott the buses and walk to work for 381 days. King was given this honour because he was chosen to lead the Montgomery Improvement Association (MIA) which coordinated the boycott. He earned that position because he was a gifted public speaker and inspired the black community to take a stand against the injustice of segregation. As a result of his assertion of this concept at the boycott, and the publicity it attracted, Martin Luther King Jr. became a prominent civil rights leader. His strategy of nonviolent protest became the model for challenging injustice. He was admired because went on to personally lead many further campaigns.

This concept is demonstrated by African American pastors, such as Martin Luther King, using their churches in Montgomery as centers to inform the black community of the boycott campaign. Martin Luther King Jr. was a pastor of the Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery. As a minister he was already a respected leader in the black community of Montgomery. The evening after the Montgomery Improvement Association was formed to co-ordinate the bus boycott, Reverend Martin Luther King gave an inspirational speech to a mass meeting at the Holt Street Baptist Church. From the church pulpit King and other black ministers inspired the African American community of Montgomery to continue the Montgomery Bus Boycott until they were desegregated.

This concept is demonstrated by the ideas that inspired Martin Luther King’s use of civil disobedience and nonviolent action to fight injustice. He was inspired by Mahatma Gandhi (1869–1948), the leader of a nationalist movement against the British rule of India. King was encouraged to read books on Gandhi’s ideas, about how to use nonviolent protest to achieve political and social change, by Howard Thurman, his professor at Boston University. Gandhi himself was inspired by American philosopher Henry Thoreau who wrote about civil disobedience. Gandhi also knew about Te Whiti Rongomai’s earlier passive resistance at Parihaka in 1880s Aotearoa. He was told of the peaceful settlement at Parihaka by two Irish visitors who had seen it.

This concept is demonstrated by the fact that the Montgomery Bus Boycott was sparked by the actions of Rosa Parks, who on the 1st of December 1955 refused to give up her seat on a segregated Montgomery bus. Rosa was a member of the Black Civil Rights organisation the NAACP who had the previous year (1954) won a landmark supreme court ruling in Brown vs Board of Education to desegregate schools. Segregation of public facilities, including buses, in Montgomery was a result of the racist and unjust treatment of black people under Jim Crow laws. Rosa and other African Americans in Montgomery, who wanted to stand up for their civil rights, wanted segregation to end. Frequent injustices, such as the murder of Emmet Till, made them more determined to rise up and make a stand.

rows: Matching – Recognising that two objects look the same (e.g. pairing socks).
Sorting – Grouping objects by colour, shape, or size.
Comparing – Noticing differences in size, height, or quantity (e.g. “This pile has more blocks”).
Sharing – Dividing objects between people, showing an early sense of quantity.
Engaging in play with quantity concepts – Filling and emptying containers, stacking blocks, or distributing pretend food.
Pointing or requesting to quantities – Indicating "more" or "less" without using number words.
Ordering – Arranging objects in a sequence (e.g., lining up toys from smallest to biggest).
Recognising patterns – Identifying and repeating sequences (e.g. red-blue-red-blue beads).
Subitising (without number words) – Instantly recognising small groups (like knowing there are two cookies without counting).
